newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Long dead Generalissimo Chiang still can't rest.
newsitem.headline: Long dead Generalissimo Chiang still can't rest.

text.p: Twenty-one years after the death of Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek, the long-serving strongman, president and icon of Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party still cannot rest in peace.

The body of Chiang, who died in 1975 without realising his goal of reclaiming power on the Chinese mainland, is embalmed in a casket now serving as tourist attraction -- while party elders and ageing relatives debate where to bury him.

The issue has become an emotional link to old glory for Chiang's erstwhile comrades and surviving family members, who propose moving the late president's body back his native China in a symbolic fulfilment of his political mission.

But reflecting the once-powerful Chiang clan's fading status under Taiwan's decade-old democratic renaissance, today's Nationalist leaders are ignoring a proposal that could complicate Taipei's already-difficult ties with Beijing.

Further denting support for a mainland burial is that the Nationalists no longer claim a sacred mission to retake China -- a popular call during Chiang's authoritarian era but one that has little legitimacy in democratic Taiwan.
Chiang's Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war to Mao Zedong's Communists.
Throughout his rule in Taiwan, the self-styled World War Two generalissimo continued to maintain that he was the legitimate ruler over all of China's historic lands, not just Taiwan.

Few Taiwan people hold that view today, preferring to take pride in their great economic and political strides on an island that after 48 years of estrangement is home to ever fewer China exiles and far higher living standards than their mainland kin.
Chiang Kai-shek has faded dramatically in relevance.
His mustachioed face smiles from Taiwan's $500 and $1,000 notes but that once-ubiquitous visage is rarely seen in public, unlike that of Sun Yat-sen, the late "father of the republic".

The burial issue reached a compromise earlier this month when a panel of Nationalist Party elders -- most wielding little political power -- agreed to bury Chiang in Taiwan but only to await an "appropriate" opportunity to transfer him to China.
Chiang Yen-shih, a member of the panel formed to settle the issue, said Madame Chiang Kai-shek, Chiang Kai-shek's widow who now resides in New York, had agreed to the proposal.
"The bottom line is that both the mainland and Taiwan are territories of the Republic of China," Chiang Yen-shih, who is unrelated to Chiang Kai-shek, said to justify the decision.

Burial in Taiwan is a hard pill to swallow for Chiang Kai-shek's sole surviving son Wego Chiang, a party elder who had first proposed moving the bodies of Chiang Kai-shek and his other son -- the late president Chiang Ching-kuo -- to China.
"Could you agree if it involved your ancestors?" Wego Chiang, 80 and ailing, asked from a hospital bed recently.
He said would stand by Madame Chiang's wishes.

Chiang Yen-shih said the Nationalist panel would meet to determine a burial ground in Taiwan for Chiang Kai-shek and Chiang Ching-kuo. But he declined to say when would be an "appropriate time" for the ultimate transfer to China.
Taiwan and China, despite a decade of increasing economic and cultural ties, remain bitter political rivals. Beijing vows to attack if Taiwan tries to declare independence.
Taipei says it wants to reunify with China eventually but maintains the right to rule Taiwan as a sovereign government before reunification.
Taiwan also says reunification would be impossible unless Beijing launches democratic reforms as Taipei has.
